Latin’s Enduring Benefits: Teachers Report Lifelong Skills From Classical Studies

A Teacher’s Journey from Comprehensive to Classics Advocate

Prof. Lesley Smith, now a professor at Oxford, recalls learning Latin at a “bog‑standard comprehensive” in Sunderland. She says the language made more sense to her than French because the local landscape is steeped in Roman history. The grammar of Latin, she argues, sharpened her understanding of other languages and provided a “career and a future” that extended beyond the classroom.

Introducing Latin as Enrichment

In a typical comprehensive school, staff were invited to add a six‑week enrichment project of personal interest. Smith chose Latin. What began as a short‑term experiment “extended into years until I retired,” she writes. The sustained programme led to the establishment of a Latin GCSE, an AS level in Classical Civilisation, and a school‑organised trip to Greece. Some pupils later pursued linguistics at university, citing the analytical skills they first honed through Latin.

Student Voices: Latin as a Living Language

Arlene Holmes‑Henderson, a Durham University professor campaigning for classics in schools, is quoted in the source as saying students “see it is living.” Smith’s former students echo this sentiment. One student surprised his parents by spotting a gerundive on a London billboard, while others reported that Latin grammar clarified aspects of English and French studies. Connections were drawn to drama, poetry, medicine and everyday life, illustrating the breadth of Latin’s influence.

Encouragement from Fellow Educators

Liz Byrne, a teacher in Letchworth, Hertfordshire, adds her perspective. After learning Latin herself, she introduced the language to her own classes, noting that “some teachers do both simultaneously.” She highlights the “endless fascination of etymology” and describes a weekly Latin poetry reading group that has persisted for more than three decades, sparked by a beloved teacher of her sons.

Practical Implications for Schools

  • Curriculum Enrichment: The source shows that a short‑term enrichment project can evolve into a permanent part of a school’s curriculum, including formal qualifications (GCSE, AS level).
  • Skill Transfer: Teachers and students report improved grammatical awareness in modern languages and enhanced analytical thinking.
  • Student Motivation: Real‑world connections—such as spotting Latin on signage—appear to boost engagement and confidence.

What Remains Uncertain

The article does not provide quantitative data on exam performance, university admission rates, or broader national trends in Latin enrolment. It also does not detail funding mechanisms, teacher training pathways, or how widespread such enrichment projects are across the UK.

How Readers Can Verify the Story

All quotations and anecdotes are drawn from a Guardian feature published on 8 January 2025. Readers can consult the original article for the full context at:

https://www.theguardian.com/education/2025/jan/08/latin-can-lay-down-skills-that-last-a-lifetime

The piece includes the perspectives of Prof. Lesley Smith, Arlene Holmes‑Henderson, and Liz Byrne, as well as details of the enrichment programme’s evolution.
